summary: Wave 2's review gave us a list. Every point on it is below, in the reviewer's own words, with what we did about it and where to check. Items still being built say so.

feedback.quote: To improve: Deploy to testnet and add the contract address to your README
feedback.did: Both demo ballots are deployed on Midnight Preprod with six real votes each. The README lists both contract addresses and every deploy, register and vote transaction. The live page reads both from the indexer and recovers 6 of 6 votes from the leaky one, 0 of 6 from the fixed one.

feedback.quote: You implemented genuine private state with implemented witnesses and a commitment/hash, exactly what a Midnight app should do.
feedback.did: We built a second contract that uses private state for a real job. Tell Desk keeps a team's full report private and puts only a commitment and the grade on the ledger. Wallets and dApp stores can read the grade by contract address.

evidence.label: Tell Desk: public ledger and private state

feedback.quote: We are not currently offering grants specifically, so please consider applying to our technical fellowship program
feedback.did: We applied to the Aliit technical fellowship with Tell as the project.

feedback.quote: Since the Midnight application requires an implementation that prioritizes privacy, tools like this help enhance the ecosystem's apps.
feedback.did: We took Tell to the apps themselves. Teams whose contracts showed a real leak in the survey got a private note with the finding and the fix, and we filed issues on Midnight's own example repositories. Replies and fixes are tracked on the adoption page.

feedback.quote: Genuinely interesting ecosystem tool, but as a business it is small.
feedback.did: We wrote down who pays and for what. The core stays free. A hosted pull-request bot for private repositories, an audit-firm license and ecosystem sponsorship are the paid parts. Each one is marked live, pilot or planned.

evidence.label: Who Tell is for, and who pays

feedback.quote: Your real substitutes are the Compact compiler itself and manual review by security firms such as Trail of Bits or Least Authority
feedback.did: We answered each substitute in turn: the compiler, audit firms, the free Web2 analyzers and OpenZeppelin's announced Compact scanner. For each one we say what it does, what Tell adds and how they work together.

feedback.quote: the closest Web2 analogues (Slither, Semgrep, Snyk) are free or sold per developer seat
feedback.did: We price the same way they do. The analyzer is free and open source. Money comes from hosted checks on private code and from audit firms, not from per-seat licenses for the scanner.

feedback.quote: the buyer pool here is the few dozen teams building on Midnight
feedback.did: The users now go beyond dApp teams. Audit firms, the Foundation's templates, wallets and dApp stores that read on-chain grades, and AI coding agents (through an MCP server) all use Tell. The privacy grade becomes something users see, and that gives teams a reason to earn a good one.

feedback.quote: if you already have a live product, active users, or revenue, we'd love to hear from you, even if you're still early and the numbers are small.
feedback.did: Tell is live: web scanner, CLI, GitHub Action and README badge. The adoption page shows the numbers as they are, small ones included: stars, repositories using the Action, outreach replies and fixes that landed. A script reads them from GitHub's public API.

evidence.label: Adoption numbers, with the fetch date

feedback.quote: We're interested in what you've learned from bringing a product to market, what challenges you're working through, and how the Midnight ecosystem might help you take the next step.
feedback.did: Below we say what we learned from putting Tell in front of teams, what is still hard, and what would help most from the Midnight ecosystem.

Tell reads any Compact contract, whatever the industry. We are adding worked examples from those sectors, starting with a supply-chain contract whose shipment record sits behind a guessable hash, and a game whose hidden move has only a few possible values. Each one comes with its fix.

feedback.quote: frontend intuitive, behaves as expected, connects to the contract end to end
feedback.did: The scanner now has share links (the contract travels inside the link and is never stored), a fix view with the proposed patch and a re-scan, a README badge, and downloads as JSON, SARIF or Markdown. Tell Desk adds a wallet flow against a new contract.

substitutes.name: The Compact compiler
substitutes.what: Makes you write disclose() wherever private data may reach the ledger. It answers whether something goes public.
substitutes.answer: Tell measures how much a disclosure gives away: a hash with four possible inputs is still a disclosure. Tell reads the compiler's own reduce-to-circuit output, so it works alongside the compiler and could become one of its passes. If the compiler adopts it, that is a good outcome for Midnight.

substitutes.name: Audit firms (Trail of Bits, Least Authority)
substitutes.what: Manual review by experts, weeks of work and priced to match. Few teams on a testnet can afford it.
substitutes.answer: Tell is not competing with them. It gives an auditor a per-circuit map of every disclosure in bits, which they can use as the privacy section of a Compact review, and it gives teams that cannot afford an audit a first pass before deploying.

substitutes.name: Slither, Semgrep, Snyk
substitutes.what: Free or per-seat static analyzers for Solidity and general code. None reads Compact or knows Midnight's dual ledger.
substitutes.answer: We copy their model rather than compete with it. The analyzer is free and open source, like Slither. Paid hosted checks cover private code, like Semgrep's and Snyk's hosted tiers. The difference is the domain: they find bugs, Tell measures privacy leaks in bits.

substitutes.name: OpenZeppelin's announced Compact scanner
substitutes.what: Security detectors for Compact from OpenZeppelin: loop bounds, assertion messages and other correctness checks.
substitutes.answer: It checks correctness and Tell checks privacy, so they complement each other. Tell's output is SARIF, so both can run in the same GitHub code scanning view, and Tell's rules could feed their detectors.

learned.title: Finding the leak is not enough
learned.text: When a team sees a finding, the next question is always how to fix it. That is why the fix view and auto-fix exist: a finding without a patch is extra work, and a verified patch is easy to say yes to.

learned.title: Privacy grades need to be seen
learned.text: A grade only on the developer's screen changes little. When a wallet or a dApp store can read it from the chain, users can see it too, and teams have a reason to earn a good one. That is the job of Tell Desk's registry.

learned.title: Approach teams privately first
learned.text: We never name a team publicly. Findings go to each team privately, with the fix, and the public page shows only anonymised outcomes. A leak in a public contract is the team's to fix, not ours to announce.

learned.title: The compiler moves fast
learned.text: Five compiler versions in one buildathon, with two output formats. Keeping up with each release is the main maintenance cost, and it is exactly what ecosystem support would pay for.

ask.title: A Tell check in Midnight's templates
ask.text: If create-mn-app and the example repositories shipped the Tell Action, every new project would be checked from its first commit.

ask.title: A stable compiler IR
ask.text: A documented, versioned form of the reduce-to-circuit output would make Tell, and any other analyzer, cheaper to maintain.

ask.title: Introductions
ask.text: Introductions to audit firms reviewing Compact, and to wallet teams that could show a privacy grade before users sign.
